title: Reviving Error Correction in Modern Deep Time-Series Forecasting
one_liner: When a neural network predicts one step ahead repeatedly, errors pile up — so train a separate tiny model to catch and fix those errors without retraining the original.
lead: Deep learning models are good at predicting the next day's weather or stock price. But in long-term forecasting, the model predicts the next day, uses that prediction as input to predict day two, uses that prediction for day three, and so on. Each wrong guess feeds into the next, causing errors to explode. This paper asks: can we add a small "error fixer" on top of any existing forecaster to reverse the damage?

paras: A trained neural network can predict tomorrow's price or temperature very well. But ask it to predict ten days ahead, and most models break. Here's why: to predict day ten, the model must first predict days one through nine. The model makes a small error on day one. Then it uses that wrong prediction to make day two's guess, so day two's error grows. By day ten, the errors have stacked so high that the forecast is nearly useless.

A naive fix might be: train the model on longer sequences so it learns to handle error buildup itself. But this is slow, expensive, and the model still struggles. The real issue is that during training, the model always sees the true past values, not its own mistakes. At prediction time, it sees only its own guesses stacked on top of each other—a world very different from what training showed it.

callout.html: Add a lightweight second model that learns to spot and fix the forecaster's mistakes, without ever retraining the first model.

paras: The paper adds a small trainable model (the corrector) that wraps any existing forecaster. This corrector never touches or retrains the original model—it only observes the original model's mistakes and learns to reverse them.
object.object: Predictions, via a learned correction layer

hidden.name: Decomposed error in trend vs. seasonal
paras: Long-term forecasts contain two main patterns: a slow-moving trend (like inflation creeping up year after year) and a repeating seasonal pattern (like summer heat or winter cold returning each year). Traditional statistical models decompose the forecast this way. The paper does the same, but for neural network errors: it measures how much the trend component is wrong and how much the seasonal component is wrong, separately.

The corrector model learns these two error signals on held-out test data—data the original forecaster has never seen. Then, at prediction time, it applies separate adjustments to the trend and seasonal parts, rather than trying to fix a blended, confusing error signal.

heat.caption: Darker means larger error across the forecast; trend and seasonal errors grow separately

reads.html: The forecast breaks into two parts: the slow-moving direction plus the repeating wiggles. Errors in each part compound differently.
Seasonal-trend decomposition isolates error modes; the corrector learns separate adjustments for each component.

paras: When a forecaster makes a long-term prediction, its errors come from two sources: it may misunderstand the overall direction (trend), or it may miss the seasonal bumps. If you try to fix both at once with one number, you confuse the learning signal. A small nudge might fix day three's seasonal wobble but wreck day five's trend.

By splitting the error into trend and seasonal, the corrector sees two clean, separate signals. It learns: 'this forecaster tends to overestimate trend by about 0.5 units per day' and 'the seasonal pattern is usually off by about 2 units.' These two learnings stay independent. When the corrector applies them, it fixes the trend slowly across all ten days and patches the seasonal spikes where they appear. Because each adjustment targets a different part of the forecast, they do not cancel each other out—both improve together.

math.words: Final forecast equals the original forecast plus a learned adjustment that depends on the trend error and the seasonal error observed in the past
math.equation: forecast_corrected = forecast_original + w_trend * error_trend + w_season * error_season

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the model predicts day 10 temperature as 72 degrees.
On held-out data, we noticed: the model typically underestimates the trend by 1 degree, and overshoots the seasonal bump by 0.5 degrees.
The raw 72 is adjusted upward (trend fix) and slightly downward (seasonal fix), moving toward reality.

math.note: The corrector does not guess on the fly; it applies offsets learned from the model's typical mistakes on unseen data.

items.html: If the corrector is trained on the same forecaster output it will later try to fix, it may learn spurious patterns. The fix: always train the corrector on held-out data the main model has never seen, or on a separate time window.

items.b: The model's error pattern changes over time.
items.html: If the forecaster's biases shift (e.g., it starts overestimating once oil prices spike), the pre-learned corrections will not match the new errors. The corrector must be retrained periodically as the real-world conditions the model sees change.

items.b: Trend and seasonal are hard to separate.
items.html: Some real-world time series do not decompose cleanly (e.g., trend and season are tangled). In such cases, the decomposition may throw away important signals, and the corrector cannot recover them.
Use held-out test data to learn the corrector. Retrain it periodically as new data arrives. On datasets where trend and seasonal patterns are clear and stable, the method works reliably.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple time-series forecaster (a 2-layer neural network that predicts the next 10 days of a synthetic sine wave plus trend). Use it to forecast out 10 steps by feeding each prediction as input to the next prediction on a test set, and measure error at each step. Train a corrector on a separate validation set by decomposing the forecaster's predictions into trend (running average) and seasonal (deviations from that average), measuring the typical error in each part, and learning simple linear weights to fix them. Apply the corrector to the test set and measure error again. The demo succeeds if errors at day 10 shrink by at least half.
demo.closing: The visual payoff: watch the test-set forecast curve bending back toward the true signal in the last few days.
